details:
Project Details — TerraVanta

TerraVanta is a web-based agricultural climate information platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in response to the challenge “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data.” Its purpose is to make climate and Earth observation data easier to understand and explore so that farmers, students, and other users can better understand environmental conditions that may affect agriculture.

The platform brings together NASA POWER climate data, NASA Terra MODIS vegetation imagery through NASA’s Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS), and Open-Meteo forecast information. Users can explore historical temperature and precipitation patterns, compare different regions, view climate indicators, examine forecast conditions, and visually compare satellite-based vegetation observations. TerraVanta also includes a Pakistan case study comparing climate patterns in Quetta and Lahore.

The project provides several features: historical climate analysis, interactive field-monitoring information, a climate risk scorecard, regional comparisons, a Pakistan-focused case study, and an NDVI evidence page. These features present environmental information through interactive maps, charts, and explanations rather than requiring users to interpret raw datasets themselves.

The intended benefit is to improve access to climate information and support agricultural awareness and planning. By helping users explore changes in temperature, precipitation, weather conditions, and vegetation observations, TerraVanta encourages more informed consideration of possible agricultural adaptation strategies. Its intended impact is to make publicly available NASA data more understandable and useful, particularly for people exploring climate-related agricultural challenges in Pakistan and other regions.

TerraVanta was developed as a web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses NASA POWER API for historical climate information, NASA GIBS for satellite imagery, Open-Meteo API for forecast and model-estimated soil-moisture information, Leaflet for interactive maps, and OpenStreetMap for map tiles. The project is hosted using GitHub Pages, with its source code maintained in a GitHub repository. No special hardware or physical field sensors were used.

The creative aspect of TerraVanta is its integration of several data sources into one accessible agricultural climate platform. Instead of presenting satellite imagery, climate records, and forecast information separately, it organizes them into connected features that allow users to explore historical conditions, monitor forecast information, and compare regions.

During development, important factors included data accessibility, geographic relevance, clarity of presentation, usability, and scientific limitations. NASA POWER provides regional gridded estimates rather than direct farm measurements; Open-Meteo soil-moisture values are model estimates rather than readings from field sensors; and NDVI indicates vegetation greenness but does not independently identify crop type, yield, or definitive crop health. TerraVanta communicates these limitations so users can interpret the information responsibly and avoid treating general indicators as guaranteed predictions or direct agricultural advice.
